title: Count Real Mailboxes
statement:
A mail server receives addresses of the form local@domain. Before delivering, it normalizes the local part only:

  • Every . in the local part is ignored, so "j.o.e" and "joe" are the same mailbox.
  • Everything from the first + in the local part up to the @ is ignored, so "joe+shop" is "joe".

The domain is used exactly as written, dots included. Given a list of emails, return how many different mailboxes actually receive mail.

examples.why: The first two both reach annlee@mail.io. The third has a different domain.
Dots are ignored only before the @. "sit.e.com" is a different domain.
The dot after the + is cut off together with the rest of the tag.

constraints: Each address has exactly one @, a non-empty local part that does not start with +, and a non-empty domain
hints: Two addresses go to the same mailbox exactly when their normalized forms are equal. So normalize, then count distinct strings.
Split at the @. Only the left side changes.
On the left side, cut at the first +, then remove every dot. Put local@domain into a set.

explain.intuition:
The question "how many different mailboxes" becomes "how many distinct strings" once every address is rewritten into the one form the server actually uses. A set does the counting.

The order of the two rules matters only a little: cut at the + first, and dots after it disappear anyway. What matters most is touching only the local part, since dots in the domain are real.
steps: Split each email at @ into local and domain.
If local contains +, keep only the part before the first one.
Add local + "@" + domain to a set and return its size.
pitfalls: Removing dots from the whole address, which merges different domains.
Cutting at the last + instead of the first.
Using replace(".", "") in JavaScript, which replaces only the first dot.

solutions.title: Normalize into a set
solutions.idea: Rewrite each address into its delivered form and count distinct forms.

solutions.title: Single character scan
solutions.idea: Build the local part character by character, stopping at + or @, skipping dots.

followups: Group the original addresses by mailbox instead of counting. What changes?
Some providers ignore dots and some do not. How would you make the rules configurable per domain?
